title: Not Plato's Republic
hookLine: don't hope for a perfect world; be content if the smallest thing goes forward (Meditations 9.29)

lines: IT MATTERS ONLY IF IT FIXES ALL?
cards: The town meeting runs all evening and ends with a vote to study the issue further. The group project has one person doing all the work. The world's problems are so big you can't even find the edge of one to hold on to.
It's easy to decide that nothing you do matters unless it fixes everything. Marcus ran an empire, and in book nine he answered that pull with a five-word line.

teach.b: He begins: the cause of all things is like a rushing river; it carries everything along. And how cheap, he says, are the little men who play at statesmanship and imagine they're doing philosophy.
Then the line, in George Long's 1862 translation: “Do not expect Plato's Republic.”
Plato wrote a whole dialogue imagining the perfect city, ruled by philosophers. Marcus, a ruler who wrote philosophy, tells himself not to expect it.
Instead, be content if the smallest thing goes forward, and don't think that outcome is a small matter. Why?
Who, he asks, can change people's beliefs? And without a change of belief, what do you get but people groaning while they pretend to obey? Force can make a law.
It can't make a heart agree. Marcus mentions rulers, Alexander and Philip among them, and says if they only played the tragic hero, no one has sentenced him to copy them.
The work of philosophy, he writes, is simple and modest; don't lead me into pomposity. He also tells himself to do what nature asks right now, without looking around to see whether anyone will know.
So the hope isn't the perfect city.
It's the next small thing, moved forward one honest inch.

how: People who take this line seriously tend to set small, concrete goals inside big problems, and count each small step as real progress rather than waiting for a complete solution.

o: Marcus's image for the cause of all things
a symbol of a life that's slipping away
a picture of anger that can't be held back

games.q: not Plato's Republic — tap the pairs.
p: the perfect city, not to be expected
be content if it goes forward

s: Marcus set out to build Plato's ideal city in Rome
he tells himself not to expect Plato's Republic, and to be content with small progress.
he says force can't change what people believe
without changed beliefs, he writes, you only get people groaning while they pretend to obey.

games.q: you're emperor. you could force a law that makes everyone behave better. what does Marcus tell himself?
o: build the perfect city, by force if needed.
be content if the smallest thing goes forward.
games.why: do not expect Plato's Republic, he writes. force can't change beliefs, so he aims for small, real progress, and calls it no small matter.

practice: Pick one problem that feels too big, in your work, your family, your town, the world, and for one breath let it be too big.

Then look for the smallest thing in it that could go forward this week: one email, one conversation, one bag of litter, one hour of help. Make it small enough that you could actually do it, and see yourself doing it.

wordCard.voice: Rushing river. Marcus's image for the cause of all things, carrying everything along; even so, he asks only that the smallest thing move forward. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the Republic, Plato's dialogue about the ideal city; the word means a constitution, a city's way of life.

carryVoice: Your line: the smallest thing. Moved forward, it's no small matter. Day six hundred eleven, done.
